title: Pranayama
one_line: The second of the six limbs, the practice of taking in the subtle power of the vital wind through rechaka, puraka, and kumbhaka in conjunction with the three bandhas, by which the mind is arrested and the diseases of body, sense organs, and mind are cured.
points: Guruji writes that there are many kinds of pranayama: Sri Shankara Bhagavadpada speaks of a thousand and explains their methods, while Swatmarama names but eight — suryabedana, ujjayi, sitkari, shitali, bhastrika, bhramari, murchha, and plavini. Of these, Guruji says only four are suitable for us.
Some pranayamas are useful for curing diseases, some for purification of the nadis, and some for the arrest of the mind, but all require that asana be practiced first.

Pranayama is not simply taking in the breath and letting it out through the nostrils; it means taking in the subtle power of the vital wind through rechaka (exhalation), puraka (inhalation), and kumbhaka (breath retention), practiced together with the three bandhas — mula bandha, uddiyana bandha, and jalandhara bandha.

Through pranayama the mind becomes arrested in a single direction and follows the movement of the breath, per the Hatha Yoga Pradipika verse that the breath in motion means the mind is moving, and the breath without motion means the mind must be motionless.

In hatha yoga there are thousands of methods of pranayama — some purify the nadis, some purify and strengthen the body, some cure diseases and purify the seven dhatus, and others lead to the cessation of the mind and knowledge of Brahman. Among these, Guruji says kumbhaka pranayama is the most important, quoting Shankara Bhagavadpada that among a thousandfold kumbhas, the pure kumbha alone is highly esteemed.

Guruji lays out rules of food, sex, and speech for the practitioner: sattvic foods are best; sour, salty, or spicy foods and vegetables consumed in quantity are unpleasant for practitioners; only half the stomach should be taken up by food, one quarter by water, and one quarter left to the movement of air; too much talk destroys the power of the tongue and speech; too much sex weakens the body, sense organs, and mind.
The place of practice should be spotlessly clean and level, have windows, and be suitable for smearing with cow dung — never in the open air, an unclean or malodorous place, a basement, or a roof.

Sweat formed during practice should be rubbed back into the body by hand, not dried in the open air, which saps the body's strength over time; per the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, rubbing the body with the perspiration of exertion produces firmness and lightness of the body.
During the period of yoga practice it is advisable to take in much milk and ghee; for the first three months, cold-water bathing and fasting are to be avoided.

Guruji quotes the Hatha Yoga Pradipika that yoga is accomplished by six things — enthusiasm, boldness, firmness, discrimination of truth, conviction, and avoidance of public gatherings — and that whether young, old, very old, sick, or debilitated, one who is vigilant attains success in all the yogas by practice.

sutra.sanskrit: Suryabhedanamujjayi sithkari shithali tatha / Bhastrika bhramari murccha plaviniti ashtakumbhakah.
sutra.translation: Suryabedana, ujjayi, sitkari, shitali, bhastrika, bhramari, murchha, and plavini are the eight kumbhakas.
